name: The Long Morning
summary: The way out is open to everyone, costs nothing, and almost nobody takes it. When somebody does, the grief of those left behind goes missing. Bettany braced for hers and was robbed of it instead.
body: Nangijala is not the last place. That much is not in dispute, which makes it unusual among everything else in this book.

Every so often somebody here stops being here. Not the Quiet — nothing like the Quiet. A person who is entirely Bright, all the way back to their own name and their own face, needing nobody to hold any piece of them, will one evening simply not be in the room. That night the northern sky lights up. The tellers say the lights are the far edge of somebody else's dawn, seen from underneath. It is a beautiful thing to say. Nobody has come back to confirm it. Not once, not ever, not a word.

The way is open to everybody and it appears to cost nothing. Remember yourself completely and you may go on. That is the requirement, the only requirement, and it has never once been observed to fail. And almost nobody goes. To understand this country you have to hold both halves of that sentence, and the second half begins with the people left in the room.

When Britt went on — young in death, bright as a coin, whole faster than anyone the tellers could name — her sister braced for the grief the way you brace for cold water. [[characters/ef25b1f0|Bettany]] is a scribe; she had done grief before, she knew the shape of her own. It never came. She remembers Britt entire — every year, every fight, the exact pitch of her singing over the wash-water — and she has never found one grain of sorrow in herself, not that night, not since. That is what broke her. Not the loss. The absence of the loss. Grief was the last thing of her sister she owned, and something took it.

Everyone bereaved by the Long Morning reports the same absence, and nearly everyone else calls it a mercy: see how gently the country lets go of its best. The bereaved learn to stop answering that. What it is like — Bettany has collected the testimony, and the wording barely varies — is coming home on the day of the funeral to find the house has been entered and exactly one thing taken, and everything else left neat, and the neighbours saying what a kind thief. She refuses to call it mercy until somebody can tell her what it is. She began [[lore/the_chronicle|the Chronicle]] to find out. You are holding it.

So the question the woken always ask, a year in, at somebody's fire, wearing the face of a person who has spotted what everybody else missed: if the door is open, and it costs nothing, why is anybody still here?

Walk the country and the answers are standing at their posts. A woman comes to the meadow for every waking because her husband has not fallen yet, and she will not go on ahead of him, and she has waited long enough now that the waiting has begun to replace her. A man on the eastern fells follows, at a distance, a shape gone to Habit that used to be his brother, walking its one faithful empty round; he will not leave a thing that still has his name in its mouth. [[characters/8c41be1e|Hearn]] came back from [[lore/the_hole_under_the_mountain|the hole under the mountain]] alone, the only one of that company who did, and going on has looked to him like getting away with it ever since; he stays, and does not get away with it, one deliberate year at a time. [[characters/cfe826c1|Jehanne]] keeps every form of a faith she stopped believing, and will not walk toward a far shore she cannot pray to; she has given up arrivals, she says, and will not be caught hoping. And [[characters/6bb1eb5a|Solveig]] could go any evening she chose — she is as whole as anyone in this country — and every evening she chooses the fire, because if she goes, who meets them?

Ask anybody in Nangijala why they are still here and they will tell you, if you have sat with them long enough. Everybody has an answer. It is the answer that makes them a person rather than a shape. Sooner or later you will find out what yours is.
